2 Thessalonians 1.summary: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ with grace and peace (2 Thessalonians 1:1-2). They say they ought always to give thanks for the Thessalonians because their faith is growing abundantly and their love for one another is increasing (2 Thessalonians 1:3). The writers boast about the church in the other churches of God for its steadfastness and faith in all its persecutions and afflictions (2 Thessalonians 1:4). They say this is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that the Thessalonians may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God for which they are suffering (2 Thessalonians 1:5). They state that God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict the believers and to grant relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:6-8). Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord, when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints and marveled at among all who have believed (2 Thessalonians 1:8-10). The writers pray that God would make the Thessalonians worthy of his calling and fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of the Lord Jesus may be glorified in them and they in him (2 Thessalonians 1:11-12).
2 Thessalonians 1.whyItMatters: Understanding the church's situation shows how the letter answers persecution by pointing to God's justice (compare Romans 12:19) rather than to retaliation, and why the hope of Christ's return is treated as a source of encouragement for the suffering.
2 Thessalonians 1.whereWeAre:
Paul and Silas brought the gospel to Thessalonica on what is traditionally called Paul's second journey; opposition arose and they were sent away by night (Acts 17:1-10). Timothy is named with them as a sender of both letters (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1).

The Thessalonian church faced persecution and afflictions from its beginning (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14), and the second letter says they continue (1:4).

Thessalonica was a major port and trade city on the Via Egnatia and was a free city under Rome. Its officials are called 'politarchs' in Acts 17:6, a title confirmed in inscriptions from the city.

The Roman Empire honored the emperor with titles and cult worship in cities such as Thessalonica. Scholars have proposed that this affected the church's trouble, but the letter does not specify the cause of the persecution.

An inscription at Delphi (a letter of Claudius, usually dated to AD 52) names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, and Acts 18:12 places Paul before Gallio at Corinth; with the eighteen months of Acts 18:11, this is used to date Paul's time in Corinth to about AD 50-52. The assurance of God's justice and the call to endurance fit a young church under pressure only months or a few years after its founding. The details of its situation help explain the intensity of the encouragement.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Writes with Silvanus and Timothy to thank, encourage and pray for the Thessalonian church. The writers' testimony ('our testimony to you') was believed by the Thessalonians (1:10).

keyFigures.name: Silvanus
keyFigures.role: Joins in the greeting and the thanks. Indicates the letter is from a team that had been with the church.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Joins in the greeting and the thanks. Part of the team known to the church.

keyFigures.name: The church of the Thessalonians
keyFigures.role: Receives thanks, praise for faith and love, and encouragement for persecution. The audience of the letter.

keyFigures.name: Those who afflict the Thessalonians
keyFigures.role: Said to be repaid by God with affliction. The passage assures the church that their treatment is not overlooked.

keyFigures.name: Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel
keyFigures.role: Will suffer eternal destruction. The passage contrasts their end with the vindication of believers.

keyFigures.name: The Lord Jesus and his mighty angels
keyFigures.role: Brings relief to the afflicted and judgment on those who do not obey the gospel; is glorified in his saints. He is the center of the hope in the chapter.

keyFigures.name: God our Father
keyFigures.role: Calls the Thessalonians, and is asked to fulfill their resolve by his power. The source of grace, judgment and strength.

keyFigures.name: Other churches of God
keyFigures.role: Hear the report of their steadfastness. They show the church's example was known.

keyThemes.explanation:
The writers give thanks because the church's faith grows abundantly and love for one another is increasing.

The chapter invites readers to see growth in faith and love as a reason for gratitude.

The Thessalonians show steadfastness and faith in all persecutions and afflictions.

The passage encourages perseverance in hardship.

keyThemes.theme: God's justice and relief at Christ's return
keyThemes.explanation:
God considers it just to repay those who afflict and to give relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed.

The chapter invites readers to trust God's justice and leave judgment to him.

On that day the Lord comes to be glorified in his saints and marveled at among all who have believed.

The passage sets believers' present suffering within a larger hope.

keyThemes.theme: Prayer that God would complete the work
keyThemes.explanation:
The writers pray that God would make the Thessalonians worthy of his calling and fulfill every resolve for good by his power.

Readers are invited to pray that God would strengthen others.

2 Thessalonians 2.summary: Paul asks the Thessalonians, concerning the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ and their being gathered to him, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed by a spirit, a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from the writers, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come (2 Thessalonians 2:1-2). He says that no one should deceive them: that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). Paul reminds them that he told them these things and that they know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time (2 Thessalonians 2:5-6). The mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way (2 Thessalonians 2:7). Then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8). His coming is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders and all wicked deception for those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth and so be saved (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10). Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness (2 Thessalonians 2:11-12). The writers give thanks for the Thessalonians, beloved by the Lord, because God chose them as the firstfruits to be saved through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, and called them through the gospel so that they may obtain the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:13-14). They are to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught by spoken word or letter (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The chapter closes with a prayer that the Lord Jesus Christ and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort their hearts and establish them in every good work and word (2 Thessalonians 2:16-17).
2 Thessalonians 2.whyItMatters: Knowing the setting helps readers see that the chapter is pastoral: it aims to calm anxiety and encourage firmness, not to provide a full timetable of future events. It also reminds readers to be careful about confident identifications that the text does not make.
2 Thessalonians 2.whereWeAre:
The first letter spoke of the coming of the Lord and the day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:11), and some Thessalonians were apparently anxious or confused about the dead in Christ and the timing. The second letter addresses a further report that the day had come.

In AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself to be placed in the Jerusalem temple; the order was not carried out before his death in AD 41 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.261-309; Philo, Embassy to Gaius). Some scholars see this as part of the background to Paul's language; the letter does not say.

Daniel 11:36 describes a king who exalts himself above every god, and Antiochus IV desecrated the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54, a deuterocanonical book not in the Protestant canon). These provide parallels for the language of 2:4.

Forged letters existed in the ancient world, and 2:2 and 3:17 suggest concern that a letter claiming to be from Paul might circulate. The letter does not say that such a letter existed.

The Thessalonians were taught about these things while Paul was with them (2:5), but the content of that teaching is not recorded. The background explains why Paul's language echoes Daniel (and, for some scholars, recent events) and why he addresses fear about the timing. It also shows the limits of what we know: the content of the earlier oral teaching, the restrainer, and the man of lawlessness are not identified.

keyFigures.name: The Thessalonian believers
keyFigures.role: Told not to be shaken, to stand firm, and to hold to the traditions. They are the audience for the teaching and prayer.

keyFigures.name: Paul and his co-writers
keyFigures.role: Teach about the day of the Lord, give thanks and pray for the church. They provide the teaching and the traditions the church is to hold.

keyFigures.name: The man of lawlessness (the lawless one, the son of destruction)
keyFigures.role: Opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, takes his seat in the temple of God, and is empowered by Satan. He represents the opposition that precedes the day of the Lord, and the Lord overcomes him.

keyFigures.name: The one who restrains
keyFigures.role: Holds back the revealing of the lawless one until he is out of the way. Part of the order of events Paul describes; identity unknown.

keyFigures.name: Satan
keyFigures.role: Works through power, false signs and wonders and deception. His activity is behind the lawless one's coming.

keyFigures.name: Those who are perishing
keyFigures.role: They are deceived and sent a strong delusion. Their fate contrasts with that of the Thessalonians.

keyFigures.name: The Lord Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth and bring him to nothing. The center of the hope in the chapter.

keyFigures.name: God and the Spirit
keyFigures.role: God chose them, called them through the gospel, and comforts them; the Spirit sanctifies. They are the source of the Thessalonians' salvation and comfort.

keyThemes.explanation:
The Thessalonians are warned not to be alarmed by messages that the day of the Lord has come.

The chapter invites readers to test claims about the end times against what they have been taught.

keyThemes.theme: Opposition to God and its end
keyThemes.explanation:
The lawless one is empowered by Satan but will be brought to nothing by the Lord's coming.

The passage points readers to the Lord's final victory.

Those who refused to love the truth are deceived and condemned, while the Thessalonians are saved through belief in the truth.

The chapter invites readers to love the truth and to be cautious about deception.

God chose the Thessalonians, called them through the gospel, and will bring them to the glory of the Lord Jesus.

The passage gives believers assurance rooted in God's initiative.

keyThemes.theme: Standing firm in what was taught
keyThemes.explanation:
The Thessalonians are to stand firm and hold to the traditions taught by word or letter.

Readers are encouraged to hold to apostolic teaching and seek God's comfort.

2 Thessalonians 3.summary: Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as it was among them, and that the writers may be delivered from wicked and evil men, for not all have faith (2 Thessalonians 3:1-2). The Lord is faithful; he will establish them and guard them against the evil one (2 Thessalonians 3:3). The writers have confidence in the Lord that the Thessalonians are doing and will do what they command, and pray that the Lord direct their hearts to the love of God and the steadfastness of Christ (2 Thessalonians 3:4-5). They command the believers in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to keep away from any brother walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition received from them (2 Thessalonians 3:6). They remind the church that they themselves were not idle but worked night and day so as not to be a burden, to give an example to imitate, although they had the right to support (2 Thessalonians 3:7-9). They recall the rule: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). They hear that some walk in idleness, not busy at work but busybodies, and command and encourage such persons to do their work quietly and earn their own living (2 Thessalonians 3:11-12). The rest are told not to grow weary in doing good (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Anyone who does not obey what is said in the letter is to be noted and avoided ('have nothing to do with him'), so that he may be ashamed, but not treated as an enemy and instead warned as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14-15). Paul closes with a prayer for peace from the Lord of peace, a greeting in his own hand as the sign in every letter of his, and a final blessing of grace (2 Thessalonians 3:16-18).
2 Thessalonians 3.whyItMatters: The background shows that the instructions are about a community's practical life and care for each other. It also helps readers apply the passage carefully, noting that it addresses people unwilling to work and not those unable.
2 Thessalonians 3.whereWeAre:
Paul worked at his trade while in Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2:9), and he was a tentmaker in Corinth with Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:3).

The first letter had already told the Thessalonians to work with their hands and to admonish the idle (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12; 5:14), so the problem apparently continued by the time of the second letter.

Apostles had the right to be supported by the churches (1 Corinthians 9:3-14), but Paul sometimes chose not to use it.

In the Greco-Roman world, manual labor was often looked down on by the elite, and the poor often relied on patrons. Some scholars suggest this may have affected expectations about work and support in the church; the letter does not say so.

Ancient letters were commonly written by secretaries, with the author adding a closing greeting in their own hand (compare 1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; for a named scribe, see Romans 16:22). The practical instruction about work and support responds to a real tension in a young church, and the personal signature may reflect concern for the authenticity of Paul's letters in light of the warning in 2:2.

keyFigures.name: Paul and his companions
keyFigures.role: Ask for prayer, give commands, point to their own example, and close with a personal greeting. Their example of work is the model for the community.

keyFigures.name: The Thessalonian believers
keyFigures.role: Asked to pray, to avoid disorderly brothers, to work, and to continue doing good. The audience for the instruction.

keyFigures.name: Brothers who walk in idleness
keyFigures.role: Commanded and encouraged to work quietly and earn their own living. Their conduct is the practical problem the chapter addresses.

keyFigures.name: Wicked and evil men
keyFigures.role: Those from whom the writers ask to be delivered. They show the danger the writers faced.

keyFigures.name: The evil one
keyFigures.role: The Lord guards the Thessalonians against him. Shows the spiritual threat behind opposition.

keyFigures.name: The Lord
keyFigures.role: Establishes and guards, directs hearts, gives peace. The source of strength.

keyFigures.name: A brother who does not obey
keyFigures.role: To be noted, avoided so that he is ashamed, and warned as a brother. Shows how discipline is to be exercised.

keyFigures.name: Others in the church (those not idle)
keyFigures.role: Told not to grow weary in doing good. They share the responsibility for the community's life.

keyThemes.theme: Prayer and trust in the faithful Lord
keyThemes.explanation:
The writers ask for prayer and affirm that the Lord is faithful and will establish and guard them.

The chapter invites readers to pray for those who proclaim the word and to trust the Lord's faithfulness.

keyThemes.theme: Honest work and not being a burden
keyThemes.explanation:
The writers worked night and day to set an example, and command those who are idle to work and earn their own living.

The passage encourages readers to support themselves where they are able.

The writers say they gave an example for the Thessalonians to imitate.

The chapter invites leaders to teach by example.

Disorderly members are to be noted and avoided so they may be ashamed, but warned as brothers and not treated as enemies.

Readers are invited to correct others in a way that seeks their restoration.

keyThemes.theme: Perseverance in doing good and peace
keyThemes.explanation:
The believers are told not to grow weary in doing good, and the Lord of peace is asked to give peace.

The passage encourages continuing in good works and seeking the Lord's peace.
